book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

chapters.relation: Karen Gaffney argues that Lost exposes ideology as a pair of glasses you do not know you are wearing, using Louis Althusser's interpellation and his distinction between repressive state apparatuses (Sawyer's outdoor cage) and ideological ones (the fake heart-rate monitor that makes Sawyer police himself inside a figurative jail). She reads the Swan button ritual, Claire 'drinking Locke's Kool-Aid,' and Desmond's 'stuck in a bloody snow globe' speech as images of being trapped inside a socially constructed worldview, and notes the viewer is interpellated too by the fake-off-island openings of seasons 2 and 3. The chapter then tracks how the show builds and dismantles the ideology of otherness - Rousseau's 'run, hide, or die,' Ana Lucia calling the Others animals, the theatrical glue and fake beard, 'Others 101' Latin lessons - until the survivor/Other border dissolves when Jack and Hurley become Jacob's successors.

chapters.file: ch21 - PART FOUR - N IS FOR NECESSITY.md
ch22 - If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where.md
chapters.relation: George Wrisley uses Lost as a testing ground against ethical subjectivism and cultural relativism: the disagreement over Sayid shooting young Ben (monster or innocent child?) motivates relativism, but the Argument from Disagreement fails for the same reason Locke and Mr. Eko's button dispute does not change what will actually happen if it goes unpushed. Simple subjectivism makes every judge infallible (the Man in Black could declare his murders right) and dissolves genuine disagreement between Jacob and his brother over killing their 'mother,' while cultural relativism makes the Dharma Initiative's torture of Sayid 'right' and would have ruled Martin Luther King Jr. wrong. He concludes that Lost's ambiguous cases - Michael's murder of Ana Lucia and Libby, Ben killing Jacob, Jack extorting Ben on the operating table - invite viewers to seek objective grounds Socratically, questioning their own moral judgments with further 'why's.

Michael Austin asks what adult children owe their fathers through Jack and Christian Shephard (the drunken-surgery cover-up, 'You don't have what it takes') and Locke and Anthony Cooper (the kidney con, the defenestration). He weighs Jane English's view that parental sacrifice creates friendship rather than debt - so Locke owed Cooper nothing, and true friends like Hurley and the crib-building Locke never keep accounts - against Sidgwick's three possible sources of filial obligation (relationship quality, biological tie, gratitude for services) and David Mellow's debt-of-gratitude argument. Austin concludes that the mutual needs of parents and children - Miles reaching for Pierre Chang in 1974, Jack and Christian's reconciliation in the church - best explain what they owe each other.

Becky Vartabedian applies W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethic of prima facie duties to Michael: at the dock his actual duty of beneficence toward the kidnapped Walt overrides fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer, but does not erase his responsibility for Ana Lucia's and Libby's murders. Because Ross requires amends rather than giving a blank check, the chapter asks whether Michael's spying as 'Kevin Johnson' aboard the Kahana - culminating in giving Jin time to escape the bomb - repairs his wrongs, or whether Walt's rejection and Michael's exile from the closing church scene show he failed to make things right on the terms of those he wronged.

Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue Lost redeems characters who stop objectifying others and instead freely 'objectify' themselves for the greater good. Kant's ban on treating persons as mere means condemns Ben's lifelong manipulation and Ben's use of Sayid as an assassin, yet autonomy justifies chosen self-sacrifice like Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission, Claire volunteering as bait for Ethan, and Jack becoming the new Jacob. Mill's utilitarianism makes Kate's shooting of the Man in Black a fair trade saving her friends, while Aristotle's virtues - respect against objectification, courage in Jack's death at the cliff, the engrained honesty of reformed con man Jim LaFleur, Kate's character-building motherhood of Aaron - complete the three-theory survey.

chapters.file: ch26 - PART FIVE - D IS FOR DESTINY.md

chapters.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost through C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory - the Lamp Post station and flight 316 (the Prince Caspian dedication page) wink at the source - with the island, like Narnia, a world of crisis and second chances entered by plane crash instead of wardrobe. Flashbacks of past failures (Kate the fugitive, Sayid the torturer, Charlie's addiction, Locke's kidney con) set up struggles for faith that he illuminates with H. Richard Niebuhr on faith as a center of value and revelation as communal, and with Levinas's claim that we become ourselves only through responsibility to the Other in community. The Jack-versus-Locke man-of-science/man-of-faith debate, Charlie's moth-cocoon trial, and Jacob and the Man in Black's black-and-white stone game map onto Aslan versus the White Witch, ending in redemption through the new community and Jack's sacrificial death.

Daniel Gallagher uses Aquinas to read Lost as a drama about mistaking finite goods for the ultimate good: Jack's hope in curing, Kate's in deceiving, Jin's in his father-in-law's employment, Locke's in Anthony Cooper, and the Virgin Mary statues full of heroin all instantiate Aquinas's approaching-Peter analogy, where we know only confusedly that someone (the perfect good) is coming toward us. Desmond's and Charlie's paralysis before the good is the sin of acedia, Rose's faith that the island itself healed her cancer is presumption, and her certainty that Bernard is alive illustrates Aquinas's claim - framed through Plato's episteme versus doxa - that faith sits midway between knowledge and opinion. The chapter closes on the harmony of faith and reason, from the Five Ways' first efficient cause to Eko's dying 'I ask for no forgiveness,' grounded in Augustine's restless heart that finds no peace until it rests in God.

Shai Biderman and William Devlin argue the character John Locke begins as an empiricist in the mold of his philosophical namesake - his boar hunting, tracking, and trebuchet-building against the hatch all follow the scientific method befitting a tabula rasa mind furnished by experience - but the miracle of his healed legs poses a 'why' that empirical explanation of 'how' cannot answer. He therefore converts to the Taoism of the Tao Te Ching: the moth-cocoon lesson to Charlie, 'I stopped looking' for Sun's ring, reading dreams and signs from the island, and finally his self-sacrifice to stop the time flashes all enact following the Way. The chapter reads the black-and-white backgammon stones, Locke's one-black-one-white eyes in Claire's dream, and Jacob versus the Man in Black as yin-yang complementarity, with empiricism and Taoism finally interdependent like the dots in each half.

chapters.file: ch30 - Keep the Needle on the Record.md
chapters.relation: Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.

chapters.file: ch31 - APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers.md
chapters.relation: Scott Parker's appendix profiles the philosophers behind Lost's namesake characters: John Locke for the survivor (blank-slate empiricism, belief tempered by tolerance, The Reasonableness of Christianity), David Hume for Desmond (causation as habitual inference, with the button press as the image of induction, plus bundle-theory skepticism about the self), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau for Danielle ('man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' private property as the root of inequality). It adds Jeremy Bentham (the alias on Locke's coffin), Kierkegaard via the Fear and Trembling Hurley finds under the Temple (Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical and the leap of faith), Dogen on zazen, Edward Said for Sayid (Orientalism and the audience's own projected savagery onto the Others), and short lives of Kate Cooper Austin, Carlyle, Rutherford, Hugo Grotius, Bakunin, Ram Dass, Edmund Burke, Hawking, Minkowski, Faraday, C. S. Lewis, and Lennon.

holes.name: Louis Althusser
holes.what: Marxist philosopher who analyzed how ideology reproduces itself by interpellating individuals through repressive state apparatuses (force) and ideological state apparatuses (religion, school, family).
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire reading of Lost runs on Althusser's concepts of ideology, interpellation, and ISA/RSA, from Sawyer's fake heart-rate monitor to Claire drinking Locke's Kool-Aid.

holes.name: Interpellation (being recruited into ideology)
holes.what: Althusser's account of how individuals are inducted into a belief system that they then take for granted as the truth without realizing they were recruited.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies interpellation to the survivors' fear of the Others, the button-pressing ritual in the Swan, and even the show's viewers.

holes.name: Othering (the socially constructed Other)
holes.what: The construction of a group as fundamentally different and inferior across an us-versus-them divide, sustained by fear and marking the marker's power as the norm.
holes.why: Chapter 20 tracks how Lost builds the ideology of otherness around the Others - savage, animal, dehumanized - and then dismantles it as socially constructed when the boundary dissolves.

holes.name: Filial Obligations (what grown children owe their parents)
holes.what: The debate over whether adult children owe their parents a debt for sacrifices and biology, or whether the ideal parent-child relationship is a friendship in which debts are out of place.
holes.why: Chapter 23 weighs Jane English's we-owe-our-parents-nothing friendship model against Sidgwick's and David Mellow's debt-of-gratitude accounts using Jack, Locke, Sawyer, and Miles.

holes.name: W.D. Ross
holes.what: British deontologist who held that morality consists of multiple self-evident prima facie duties whose relative weight must be sorted into an actual duty in each situation.
holes.why: Chapter 24 evaluates Michael's betrayal and attempted atonement entirely through Ross's framework of prima facie duties, actual duty, guilt, and moral risk.

holes.name: Prima Facie Duties
holes.what: Ross's plural set of self-evident duties - fidelity, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, noninjury - that bind unless overridden by a more pressing duty in the situation.
holes.why: Chapter 24 sorts Michael's rescue of Walt against his duties to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer, asking whether his freighter espionage and saving Jin count as making amends.

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and literary philosopher whose theory of myth as embodied meaning (rather than abstract allegory) underlies the Narnia chronicles.
holes.why: Chapter 27 reads Lost as Lewisian myth - Cuse and Lindelof's stated model - applying Lewis's myth-not-allegory view, his Narnia parallels, and his own atheist-to-faith journey mirrored in Jack.

holes.name: H. Richard Niebuhr
holes.what: Christian ethicist who saw faith as the center of value that organizes a life and revelation as an ongoing, communal reinterpretation of experience.
holes.why: Chapter 27 uses Niebuhr's Faith on Earth and The Meaning of Revelation to frame the survivors' move from suspicion to trust and their redemption within community.

holes.name: Myth versus Allegory
holes.what: Lewis's view that fantasy worlds communicate theological meaning through the story itself, so the message cannot be dissected from the narrative as in coded allegory.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues Lost, like Narnia, is myth rather than allegory, so questions about the show's meaning must return to the episodes themselves rather than a decoded thesis.

holes.name: Edward Said
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist whose Orientalism argued that Western representations of the 'Orient' construct a dehumanized Other to justify domination.
holes.why: Chapter 31 profiles Said as Sayid Jarrah's namesake and applies Orientalism to the audience's projection of savagery onto the Others and the terrorist labeling of Sayid.
